items.title: Owners are fighting heritage designation for a 1917 Port Credit bungalow and a 1908 Streetsville building
items.summary: City staff recommends heritage status for 1917 Port Credit bungalow and 1908 Streetsville commercial building. The property was first proposed for designation in 2024 due to its architectural, historical and physical design and values. Mississauga city staff are recommending that council grant heritage protection to two historic buildings in the city despite objections from their owners. The recommendation to designate the two properties, 1 Godfrey’s Lane in Port Credit and 20 Thomas St. in Streetsville, is coming to the general committee meeting on Nov. 18. While both properties are currently listed on the city’s heritage registry, the city has until Jan 1, 2027, to formally designate them as heritage under Ontario’s More Homes Built Faster Act. Once removed from the registry, the properties cannot be re-listed for five years. Under the provincial rule, passed to expedite housing development, cities must formally designate a listed property as heritage within two years. Currently, listed properties are only required to give the city a 60 days’ notice before demolition. The documents provided by the city do not disclose what the property owners intend to do and if there are any specific redevelopment plans. The debate about this 1917 former lakeside summer bungalow first began in February 2024 when council first moved to designate the property as heritage. At that time, owners John Scott Bagby and Catherine Bagby formally objected to the designation which led council to defer the decision in September 2024.

items.title: Developers to fight Mississauga’s data centre moratorium at Ontario Land Tribunal
items.summary: Two developers will fight Mississauga’s one-year pause on data centres at the Ontario Land Tribunal. Industrial real estate company Prologis and real estate developer Montcrest Asset Management have both filed appeals with the Ontario Land Tribunal over Mississauga’s temporary ban on large-scale data centres. A provincial body, the tribunal adjudicates matters related to land use planning and can override municipal decisions. Amid a public outcry, Mississauga councillors passed a bylaw effectively banning the construction of large-scale data centres for up to two years while the city studies the issue. Many communities have raised concerns about the massive centres’ potential water consumption, electricity use, noise and air quality. Data centres don’t require a large number of employees once they are constructed. Data centres have been around for decades, and are needed to store and process digital information such as Google Maps, online banking and social media. During the AI boom, the need for new centres has vastly increased. After Prologis proposed a two-storey data centre for vacant land they own on Tenth Line West in the Meadowvale Business Park, just south of Highway 401, the community packed into a community town hall. Over 200 people attended, and at times, the meeting got heated with frustrated residents trying to get questions answered. Montcrest doesn’t have a planning application for a data centre in Mississauga at this time, a City of Mississauga spokesperson told INSAUGA Canada. But Montcrest Asset Management owns eight acres of industrial land on Tahoe Boulevard near Toronto Pearson Airport.

items.title: Fines set to triple for drivers of excessively loud cars in Ontario
items.summary: The Ontario government intends to increase the minimum fine from $60 to $200 for drivers whose excessively noisy cars disrupt neighbourhoods and businesses across the province, the transportation minister announced Wednesday morning in Mississauga. ” Sarkaria added that families “shouldn’t have to put up with this excessive noise outside their homes” at all hours of the night and businesses should not have their activity disrupted by the illegal behaviour either. “Extreme noise is disruptive to communities and drowns out vital emergency sirens and pedestrian warnings while distracting drivers and delaying reaction times,” Sarkaria told reporters outside Peel Regional Police headquarters in Mississauga. ” Tedjo, sworn in on Monday night as Mississauga’s eighth mayor, said excessive noise caused by cars racing on city streets and engaged in other illegal behaviour “is a quality of life issue” in Mississauga and across Ontario. He added it has frustrated residents “every day” who’ve had to put up with the noisy vehicles and associated dangers as they try to sleep at night or go about their routines. Brown said the behaviour of “reckless drivers” has threatened the “peace and tranquility” of neighbourhoods across the region.

items.title: Meet two Mississauga founders rethinking the way money moves
items.summary: Two FinTech founders in Mississauga are taking aim at the complicated infrastructure behind international payments. Gharsa Amin, founder and CEO of Kavodax, and Gezim Ramabaja, founder and CEO of Zpayd, are approaching the problem from different corners of the financial industry. One is using blockchain technology to speed up international transfers, while the other is building the connections that allow financial institutions to offer bill payments globally. Both companies have tapped into Mississauga’s startup ecosystem for mentorship, industry connections, and support in bringing their products to market. BetaKit spoke with the founders about what it takes to break into the financial industry, bring new payment technologies to market, and build a business in Mississauga. When Gharsa Amin’s grandmother fell ill in Germany, she sent money from Canada to help support her. The transfer took five days, passed through multiple banking clearances, and incurred foreign exchange fees of approximately three to four percent. Her grandmother also had to visit the bank in person to access the funds. “Having worked in digital banking, compliance, and technology, I knew there had to be a better way,” Amin said. “You don’t necessarily need to build the next major financial institution. ” She founded Kavodax in 2025 to tackle the delays and costs of international payments, particularly for small and medium-sized businesses that regularly pay overseas suppliers and contractors.

items.title: Michelin-recommended restaurant opens location soon in Square One, Mississauga
items.summary: A Michelin-recommended restaurant will open next month in Square One Shopping Centre in Mississauga. PAI, a Thai restaurant frequented by celebrities in Toronto, will open the new location on Dec. 15, the restaurant announced this week. Since opening in 2014, PAI has become known as one of Toronto’s best Thai restaurants. The Mississauga location is the first outside Toronto. Founded by Chef Nuit Regular and Jeff Regular, PAI is named after the Thai village where the couple opened their first restaurant, the Michelin recommendation states. Alongside PAI favourites, the Square One location will be the first to introduce a collection of new menu items, including Miang Pla (Thai grilled fish platter), Yum Yai salad, and Sakoo Sai Moo dumplings, PAI said. The new dishes are expected to launch first at Square One before being introduced at other PAI locations at a later date in the new year. “We’ve been looking forward to opening our doors at Square One and finally sharing what we’ve been working on with the Mississauga community,” said Chef Nuit Regular, executive chef and co-founder of PAI. “We’re introducing some new dishes for the first time here, alongside the PAI favourites our guests know and love. ” Beyond the menu, the Square One location will pay homage to where PAI’s story first began: The Curry Shack, the very first restaurant Chef Nuit Regular and Jeff opened in Pai, Thailand.

items.title: #NoGoodWay Day Campaign Turns Mississauga's Clock Tower Yellow to Retire the R-word
items.summary: According to motionball for Special Olympics, Mississauga's clock tower and city hall will be illuminated yellow on Nov. 18 to mark the national #NoGoodWay Day campaign. The organization says the campaign, running Nov. 4 to Nov. 18, aims to promote inclusive language for people with intellectual disabilities and end the casual use of the R-word. Motionball co-founder Paul Etherington said in a press release that Canadians can use their voices to challenge stereotypes and help build communities where people with intellectual disabilities are treated with respect and dignity. The organization is asking participants to wear yellow, sign an online pledge for inclusive language, and share videos of themselves symbolically destroying the R-word by tearing, deleting or erasing it. Mississauga joins other cities lighting landmarks yellow for the campaign, according to motionball.

items.title: Montcrest Becomes Second Company to Challenge Mississauga's Data Centre Moratorium at Tribunal
items.summary: According to Global News, Mississauga's one year ban on data centre construction is facing a second challenge at the Ontario Land Tribunal, this time from Toronto based real estate investment firm Montcrest Asset Management. The outlet reports Montcrest wants to build a data centre near Eglinton Avenue East and Tahoe Boulevard and is asking the tribunal to exempt its project from the moratorium. This comes as Prologis, an American warehouse developer, is separately challenging the same ban with the tribunal, according to Global News. Mississauga became one of the first Canadian cities to approve a one year data centre moratorium, which took effect in September after a unanimous council vote led in part by councillor turned mayor Alvin Tedjo. Tedjo said ahead of the vote that there were concerns about power consumption, heat islands and noise, Global News reported.

items.title: Prologis takes Mississauga to OLT over data centre moratorium
items.summary: An American logistics and warehouse developer is appealing the City of Mississauga’s one-year moratorium on data centre development, arguing the temporary ban lacks a sound planning rationale and has delayed a proposed project. San Francisco-based Prologis filed an appeal with the Ontario Land Tribunal in November, challenging the city’s interim control bylaw, which took effect in September following a unanimous council vote. The company applied in 2025 to build a two-storey, 220,000-sq. ft. data centre on former farmland near Tenth Line and Argentia Road in Mississauga. “After careful consideration of Council’s decision and the options available to us, Prologis has filed an appeal with the Ontario Land Tribunal regarding the City of Mississauga’s Interim Control By-law,” Global News reported. “Our commitment to Mississauga remains unchanged. ” Mississauga council imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centre development on Jul. 29, giving municipal staff a chance to prepare a report on potential impacts of facilities. Residents opposed to data centre development raised questions about the scale of operations, impact of water resources, electricity use and noise. ” “After careful consideration of council’s decision and the options available to us, Prologis has filed an appeal with the Ontario Land Tribunal regarding the City of Mississauga’s Interim Control By-law,” the company said in a statement.

items.title: Mississauga council sworn in — new mayor’s 1st directive is tax freeze
items.summary: Mayor Alvin Tedjo pledges affordability, economic growth and innovation at city hall as Mississauga kicks off its 2026-2030 term. Mississauga’s city council, newly elected for the 2026-30 term, at the inaugural ceremony on Nov. 16. Mississauga’s newly elected city council was sworn into office on Nov. 16 at the Living Arts Centre, marking the start of the 2026-30 term. Along with Mayor Alvin Tedjo, nine incumbent councillors and two newcomers took their declarations of office before a nearly full main auditorium. Tedjo received prolonged applause and a standing ovation from the audience and council colleagues after receiving the mayor’s chain of office — the ceremonial regalia presented to a mayor upon taking office — and during his inaugural address. Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services’ pipe and drum band performed at the inaugural ceremony on Nov. 16. The ceremony opened with a band procession by Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services’ pipe and drum band, a national anthem performance by Catherine and Chloe Tiongson and an Indigenous drum circle performed by Little Creek Singers . An Indigenous drumming circle at the inaugural ceremony by Little Creek Singers to give Indigenous blessings.
